title: Periodic Properties and Variations of Properties – Physical and Chemical
tagline: Understand periodic trends and how atomic structure governs element behaviour.

sourceNote.thirdParty: ICSE Class 10 Chemistry syllabus scope (board-prescribed topics for the named chapter); content independently authored for Target95 BoardPrep.
sourceNote.boardprep: Original explanations, examples, figure descriptions and practice questions drafted for revision; not copied from textbooks or question banks.

overview.intro: The modern periodic table arranges elements by increasing atomic number so that recurring patterns in properties become predictable. Periodic properties such as atomic size, ionisation potential, electron affinity, electronegativity and metallic character vary in regular ways across periods and down groups because of changes in nuclear charge and number of shells. Mastering these trends helps in comparing elements, predicting bonding and explaining chemical reactivity in ICSE examinations.

facts.label: Key trends
facts.value: Atomic radius, IP, EA, EN, metallic/non-metallic character

facts.label: Across a period
facts.value: Nuclear charge increases, size generally decreases

facts.label: Down a group
facts.value: Number of shells increases, size generally increases

learningOutcomes: State the basis of the modern periodic table and define periodicity.
Explain variation of atomic radius across a period and down a group.
Compare ionisation potential, electron affinity and electronegativity trends.
Relate metallic and non-metallic character to position in the periodic table.
Apply periodic trends to predict relative properties of given elements.

blocks.text: The modern periodic law states that the physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers. When elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number, elements with similar valence-shell configurations recur at regular intervals, producing groups with similar chemical behaviour.

Periods are horizontal rows indicating the number of occupied electron shells, while groups are vertical columns indicating related valence-electron patterns. Periodicity arises because similar outer electronic configurations repeat after definite intervals of atomic number.

items: Atomic number (Z) is the fundamental property for classification, not atomic mass.
Elements in the same group show similar chemical properties due to similar valence electrons.
A period corresponds to the filling of a particular principal energy level.
Position of an element helps predict its valency, bonding type and reactivity.

learn.title: Atomic Radius and Related Size Trends

blocks.text: Atomic radius is commonly described as the distance from the nucleus to the outermost shell of an atom. Across a period from left to right, atomic radius generally decreases because the nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell, pulling the electron cloud closer.

Down a group, atomic radius increases as each successive element has an additional electron shell. Increased shielding by inner electrons reduces the effective attraction of the nucleus for outer electrons, so the atom becomes larger.

items.text: Across Period 3: Na > Mg > Al > Si > P > S > Cl (general decrease in atomic size).
items.note: Increasing nuclear charge in the same shell contracts the atom.

items.text: Down Group 1: Li < Na < K < Rb in atomic radius.
items.note: Addition of shells outweighs increased nuclear charge.

learn.title: Ionisation Potential, Electron Affinity and Electronegativity

blocks.text: Ionisation potential (ionisation energy) is the energy required to remove the most loosely bound electron from an isolated gaseous atom. It generally increases across a period due to decreasing atomic size and increasing nuclear attraction, and decreases down a group as the outer electron is farther from the nucleus.

Electron affinity is the energy change when an electron is added to a neutral gaseous atom, while electronegativity is the tendency of an atom to attract shared electrons in a bond. Both generally increase across a period and decrease down a group, with important exceptions explained by electronic configuration and atomic size.

items.meaning: Energy needed to remove an electron from a gaseous atom.
Energy change associated with gaining an electron by a gaseous atom.
Relative tendency to attract a shared pair of electrons in a covalent bond.

blocks.text: Metallic character is associated with the tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions. Across a period, metallic character decreases and non-metallic character increases because atoms hold valence electrons more strongly. Down a group, metallic character generally increases as valence electrons are more easily lost.

These trends explain why alkali metals are highly reactive metals, halogens are reactive non-metals, and noble gases are largely unreactive. Periodic position therefore provides a quick guide to expected chemical behaviour.

learn.title: Using Trends in Comparisons and Predictions

blocks.text: In examination questions, periodic trends are applied to arrange elements in increasing or decreasing order of a property, justify the choice of the most metallic or most electronegative element, or predict the nature of oxides and bonding. Answers should refer to nuclear charge, number of shells and effective attraction rather than stating the trend alone.

When comparing elements, first identify whether they belong to the same period or the same group. This determines which factor dominates: change in nuclear charge within the same shell across a period, or change in number of shells and shielding down a group.

items: Same period comparison: emphasise increasing nuclear charge.
Same group comparison: emphasise increasing shells and shielding.
Link low ionisation energy with metallic behaviour and easy cation formation.
Link high electronegativity with strong attraction for shared electrons.

keyPoints: Modern periodic table is arranged by increasing atomic number and reflects periodicity of properties.
Atomic radius generally decreases across a period and increases down a group.
Ionisation potential and electronegativity generally increase across a period and decrease down a group.
Metallic character decreases across a period and increases down a group.
Trend explanations must refer to nuclear charge, shells and shielding.
Elements in the same group have similar valence configurations and related chemistry.
Periodic trends help predict reactivity, bonding and nature of oxides.
Exceptions exist, but general trends guide most ICSE comparisons.
Position in the table indicates valence electrons and likely ion formation.
Clear reasoning is as important as stating the correct order of elements.
examFocus: Define periodic properties and state the modern periodic law accurately.
Arrange given elements in order of size, ionisation potential or electronegativity with reasons.
Distinguish trends across a period from trends down a group.
Explain metallic and non-metallic character using electron loss or gain tendency.
Support answers with nuclear charge, number of shells and shielding.
Avoid vague statements; name the property and direction of variation clearly.
Use correct terminology: ionisation potential, electron affinity, electronegativity.

vocabulary.meaning: Repetition of similar properties at regular intervals when elements are arranged by atomic number.
Number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, used to arrange the modern periodic table.
A measure of the size of an atom, related to the distance to its outermost shell.
Energy required to remove the most loosely bound electron from a gaseous atom.
Energy change when a neutral gaseous atom gains an electron.
Tendency of an atom in a bond to attract shared electrons towards itself.
Positive charge of the nucleus due to protons, influencing attraction for electrons.
Reduction in effective nuclear attraction on valence electrons due to inner shells.
Electrons in the outermost shell that take part in bonding and reactions.
Tendency of an element to lose electrons and show metallic properties.
Tendency of an element to gain or share electrons and show non-metallic properties.
A vertical column in the periodic table containing elements with similar valence configurations.

questions.prompt: The modern periodic table is arranged in order of increasing:
questions.answer: atomic number
questions.explanation: Elements are placed by increasing atomic number so that properties show periodicity.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse the modern basis with Mendeleev’s atomic mass arrangement.

questions.prompt: Across a period from left to right, atomic radius generally:
questions.answer: decreases
questions.explanation: Increasing nuclear charge in the same shell pulls electrons closer, reducing atomic size.
questions.commonMistake: Remember shells remain the same across a period while nuclear charge increases.

questions.prompt: Which factor mainly causes atomic radius to increase down a group?
options: Increase in number of electron shells
questions.answer: Increase in number of electron shells
questions.explanation: Each step down a group adds a new shell, increasing atomic size despite higher nuclear charge.
questions.commonMistake: Do not attribute the increase down a group to nuclear charge alone.

questions.prompt: Ionisation potential generally increases across a period because:
options: nuclear attraction for valence electrons increases
questions.answer: nuclear attraction for valence electrons increases
questions.explanation: Smaller size and higher nuclear charge make electron removal more difficult across a period.
questions.commonMistake: Across a period shells do not increase; attraction becomes stronger.

questions.prompt: The tendency of an atom in a covalent bond to attract shared electrons is called:
questions.answer: electronegativity
questions.explanation: Electronegativity measures attraction for shared electrons within a bond.
questions.commonMistake: Electron affinity refers to gaining an electron by an isolated gaseous atom.

questions.prompt: Down a group, metallic character generally:
questions.answer: increases
questions.explanation: Valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and more easily lost down a group.
questions.commonMistake: Metallic character is linked to ease of electron loss.

questions.prompt: Which property generally decreases down a group?
questions.answer: Electronegativity
questions.explanation: Attraction for bonding electrons decreases as atomic size increases down a group.
questions.commonMistake: Atomic radius and shells increase down a group.

questions.prompt: For elements in the same period, the most important reason for decreasing size is:
options: increase in shielding by inner shells
increase in nuclear charge with same number of shells
questions.answer: increase in nuclear charge with same number of shells
questions.explanation: Greater nuclear charge pulls the same electron shell inward across a period.
questions.commonMistake: Shielding changes little across a period because inner shells remain the same.

questions.prompt: Elements in the same vertical column of the periodic table form a ________.
questions.answer: group
questions.explanation: A vertical column is called a group and contains elements with similar valence configurations.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse groups (vertical) with periods (horizontal).

questions.prompt: The energy required to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom is called ________.
questions.answer: ionisation potential
questions.explanation: Ionisation potential measures how strongly an atom holds its outer electron.
questions.commonMistake: Write the full term clearly; electron affinity is a different property.

questions.prompt: Across a period, non-metallic character generally ________.
questions.answer: increases
questions.explanation: Atoms more readily gain or attract electrons as nuclear attraction increases across a period.
questions.commonMistake: Link the trend to decreasing atomic size and stronger nuclear pull.

questions.prompt: State the modern periodic law.
questions.answer: The modern periodic law states that the physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.
questions.explanation: This law explains why arranging elements by atomic number produces repeating patterns of properties.
questions.commonMistake: Mention atomic number, not atomic mass.

questions.prompt: Why does atomic radius decrease across a period?
questions.answer: Across a period, electrons are added to the same shell while nuclear charge increases. The stronger attraction pulls the electron cloud closer to the nucleus, so atomic radius generally decreases.
questions.explanation: The key comparison is increasing nuclear charge with no increase in number of shells.
questions.commonMistake: Include both nuclear charge and same shell in the reason.

questions.prompt: Explain why ionisation potential decreases down a group.
questions.answer: Down a group, each element has an additional electron shell so the valence electrons are farther from the nucleus. Increased shielding by inner electrons reduces effective nuclear attraction, making it easier to remove an outer electron and lowering ionisation potential.
questions.explanation: Distance and shielding together explain the easier loss of valence electrons.
questions.commonMistake: Do not give the trend without the shell/shielding explanation.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between electron affinity and electronegativity.
questions.answer: Electron affinity is the energy change when an isolated gaseous atom gains an electron, whereas electronegativity is the tendency of an atom to attract shared electrons in a chemical bond. Electron affinity is a measurable energy term for an atom, while electronegativity is a comparative property in bonded state.
questions.explanation: Both relate to attraction for electrons but in different contexts.
questions.commonMistake: Avoid using the two terms as exact synonyms.

questions.prompt: Describe the variation of metallic character in the periodic table and give reasons.
questions.answer: Metallic character decreases across a period from left to right because increasing nuclear charge and decreasing atomic size make it harder for atoms to lose valence electrons. Down a group, metallic character increases because additional shells and greater shielding reduce the effective attraction on valence electrons, so they are lost more easily. Thus elements on the left and lower parts of the table are more metallic, while those on the right and upper parts are more non-metallic.
questions.explanation: The explanation links electron-loss tendency to size, nuclear charge and shielding.
questions.commonMistake: State both directions (across and down) with reasons for each.

questions.prompt: How do atomic radius, ionisation potential and electronegativity vary across Period 3? Explain.
questions.answer: Across Period 3, atomic radius generally decreases because nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell, increasing attraction. Ionisation potential generally increases as smaller atoms hold valence electrons more tightly. Electronegativity also generally increases because atoms have a stronger tendency to attract shared electrons. These related trends reflect increasing effective nuclear attraction from sodium to chlorine.
questions.explanation: All three trends arise from the same underlying change in nuclear charge and atomic size.
questions.commonMistake: Mention the common reason instead of treating each trend as unrelated.

questions.prompt: An element A is in Group 1 and Period 3, while element B is in Group 17 and Period 3. Compare their atomic size, metallic character and electronegativity with reasons.
questions.answer: Element A (sodium) has larger atomic size, higher metallic character and lower electronegativity than element B (chlorine) in the same period. A has lower effective nuclear attraction on its valence electron and tends to lose it easily, showing metallic behaviour. B has higher nuclear charge, smaller size and stronger attraction for electrons, so it is highly electronegative and non-metallic. The comparison is explained by increasing nuclear charge across the same period.
questions.explanation: Same-period comparison highlights the effect of increasing nuclear charge from left to right.
questions.commonMistake: Identify the direction across the period clearly for each property.

questions.prompt: Three elements X, Y and Z belong to the same group with X above Y and Y above Z. Predict the order of atomic radius and ionisation potential, giving reasons.
questions.answer: Atomic radius increases in the order X < Y < Z because each successive element has an additional electron shell. Ionisation potential decreases in the order X > Y > Z because valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded in lower elements, so they are removed more easily.
questions.explanation: Down a group, added shells dominate the trends in size and ease of electron removal.
questions.commonMistake: Do not reverse the ionisation potential order when size increases.

questions.prompt: Element P has low ionisation potential and element Q has high electronegativity. Predict the likely positions of P and Q in the periodic table and the type of bond they may form.
questions.answer: P is likely to be a metal on the left side and lower part of the periodic table, where electrons are lost easily. Q is likely to be a non-metal on the right side and upper part, where atoms strongly attract electrons. Such elements commonly form an ionic bond by transfer of electrons from P to Q.
questions.explanation: Property-based reasoning connects periodic position to bonding behaviour.
questions.commonMistake: Base the prediction on both properties, not just one of them.

questions.prompt: A student states that chlorine is more metallic than sodium because chlorine has higher atomic number. Evaluate this statement using periodic trends.
questions.answer: The statement is incorrect. Although chlorine has a higher atomic number, sodium and chlorine are in the same period where metallic character decreases from left to right. Sodium readily loses an electron and is highly metallic, whereas chlorine has smaller atomic size, higher ionisation potential and higher electronegativity, so it tends to gain an electron and is non-metallic. Periodic position and effective nuclear attraction, not atomic number alone, determine metallic character.
questions.explanation: The evaluation must correct the reasoning and compare the relevant periodic properties.
questions.commonMistake: Higher atomic number within a period does not imply greater metallic character.

questions.prompt: Explain how knowledge of periodic trends helps in predicting whether an element will form a positive ion or a negative ion.
questions.answer: Elements with low ionisation potential and larger atomic size, usually metals on the left or lower part of the table, tend to lose electrons and form positive ions. Elements with high electronegativity and strong attraction for electrons, usually non-metals on the right and upper part, tend to gain or share electrons and may form negative ions in ionic compounds. Thus periodic trends provide a basis for predicting likely ion formation.
questions.explanation: Ion formation is linked to ease of electron loss or gain indicated by periodic properties.
questions.commonMistake: Relate the prediction to specific properties rather than memorised charges alone.
